album: We Insist! Max Roach's Freedom Now Suite
label: Candid
rationale: The defining political statement of the hard-bop era: a five-part suite on slavery, emancipation, and African independence, recorded weeks after the Sharpeville massacre and at the height of the sit-in movement. Penguin Guide crown + Core Collection, five stars from AllMusic, and 2022 induction into the National Recording Registry. Session gravity is enormous — Coleman Hawkins guesting on 'Driva' Man', Booker Little, Julian Priester, Abbey Lincoln's career-defining vocals — and it sits directly in the lineage of the canonized Mingus works (Black Saint, Ah Um).

personnel_record.notes: Two sessions, August 31 and September 6, 1960; released January 1961 on Candid. Which tracks belong to which session date is not stated in sources consulted. Style note: AllMusic tags it Hard Bop; Wikipedia calls it avant-garde jazz with free-jazz moments (end of 'Tears for Johannesburg', the 'Protest' screams) — a fuzzy-edge case the council should weigh, but it swings and is compositionally through-written. Name variants flagged: Schenk/Schenck, Mantilla/Matillo, du Vall/Duvail. iTunes match is the 2024 Candid MONO remaster (5 tracks, 1960 copyright).

ballot.album: Max Roach — We Insist! Max Roach's Freedom Now Suite (1960)

scope_check.boundary_note: The 1960 recording is within the window; the live issue is whether the wordless vocal abstraction in "Triptych: Protest" and the freer climax of "Tears for Johannesburg" constitute excluded free-jazz, or remain borderline elements within a structured hard-bop/protest suite.

ballot.case_for: This has an unusually complete canon case: the dossier cites a Penguin Guide Crown and Core Collection designation, AllMusic's five-star rating, and 2022 National Recording Registry induction, evidence of recognition across critical and institutional traditions. It is Max Roach's defining political statement and a foundational Civil Rights-era jazz suite, with Abbey Lincoln's performance—especially the Roach-Lincoln duet "Triptych"—making its argument inseparable from its musical force. Its personnel joins Roach, Lincoln, Booker Little, Julian Priester, Babatunde Olatunji, and Coleman Hawkins on "Driva Man," giving the record both extraordinary session gravity and a cross-generational account of jazz history (dossier S1–S2).
ballot.case_against: A strict application of the excluded free-jazz gate can reasonably object that "Triptych: Protest" and portions of "Tears for Johannesburg" suspend conventional harmonic, melodic, and swinging frameworks for screams, percussion, and collective intensity; these are not merely adventurous hard-bop solos. Even if the suite is largely composed and organized, a cold listener may experience those passages as abrasive and unrepresentative of the canon's intended post-bebop discovery path. The dossier also leaves side-two percussion assignments inferred and does not map individual tracks to the two recording dates, though those documentation gaps are secondary to the stylistic question.
ballot.disagreement: Reference 1 treats the free-form passages as a genuine free-jazz boundary requiring a scope_call; Reference 2 judges the suite's through-composed hard-bop architecture sufficient to pass scope and rates it consensus_core. Both agree that, if admissible, it is must-have in importance.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John make the free-jazz boundary ruling explicitly; if embedded avant-garde passages remain admissible, this should be treated as a must-have core record.
